_about: SkillLens quiz bank. Multiple choice; answer = 0-based index of the correct option (options are shuffled per quiz). difficulty easy/medium/hard = junior/mid/senior level. Topics: python, csharp, sql, oop, algorithms.

questions.question: What does len([1, [2, 3], 4]) return?
questions.explanation: The list has three elements: 1, the nested list [2, 3], and 4. len counts top-level elements only.

questions.question: Which of these types is immutable?
questions.explanation: Tuples cannot be changed after creation; lists, dicts and sets can be modified in place.

questions.question: What is the result of 7 // 2 in Python 3?
questions.explanation: // is floor division, so 7 // 2 is 3. A single / would give 3.5.

questions.question: What does [x * 2 for x in range(4) if x % 2 == 0] produce?
questions.explanation: range(4) gives 0, 1, 2, 3; the filter keeps 0 and 2; doubling them gives [0, 4].

questions.question:
def f(a, items=[]):
    items.append(a)
    return items

What does f(1); f(2) return on the second call?
questions.explanation: Default arguments are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so the same list is reused across calls.

questions.question: Which keyword handles an exception raised inside a try block?
questions.explanation: Python uses try / except. catch is used in languages such as Java and C#.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a 'with open(path) as f:' block?
options: It closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs
It opens the file in binary mode
It locks the file for other programs
questions.explanation: with uses a context manager; the file's __exit__ method closes it when the block ends, including on exceptions.

questions.question: What does d.get('k', 0) return when the dictionary d has no key 'k'?
questions.explanation: dict.get returns the default value (here 0) when the key is missing, instead of raising KeyError.

questions.question: What is printed by: a = [1, 2]; b = a; b.append(3); print(a)?
questions.explanation: b = a does not copy the list; both names refer to the same object, so the change is visible through a.

questions.question: What does a function containing 'yield' return when it is called?
options: A list of all yielded values
questions.explanation: Calling a generator function returns a generator; values are produced lazily when it is iterated.

questions.question: Which statement makes the function sqrt from the math module available as sqrt?
questions.explanation: The syntax is 'from module import name'.

questions.question: What is the value of 'python'[1:4]?
questions.explanation: Slicing includes the start index and excludes the end index: characters at 1, 2, 3 are 'y', 't', 'h'.

questions.question: What does the expression {1, 2, 3} & {2, 3, 4} evaluate to?
questions.explanation: & on sets is intersection: the elements present in both sets.

questions.question: What does print(type(3.0)) display?
questions.explanation: 3.0 has a decimal point, so it is a float. Python has no separate double type.

questions.question: Why do CPU-bound Python threads (CPython) usually not run faster on several cores?
options: Threads are not supported in Python
The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time
Each thread gets its own copy of every variable
The operating system limits Python to one core
questions.explanation: In CPython the GIL serialises bytecode execution; for CPU-bound work use multiprocessing (or native code that releases the GIL).

questions.question: What is the main effect of defining __slots__ in a class?
options: Instances get a fixed set of attributes and no per-instance __dict__, saving memory
questions.explanation: __slots__ replaces the per-instance dictionary with fixed slots, which saves memory and blocks adding new attributes.

questions.question: Why is functools.wraps used inside a decorator?
options: To make the decorated function run faster
To copy the wrapped function's name, docstring and other metadata to the wrapper
questions.explanation: Without wraps, the decorated function would report the wrapper's __name__ and __doc__, which confuses debugging and tools.
members is a class attribute, so every instance appends to the same shared list. Initialise it in __init__ to get one list per instance.

questions.question: Which character starts a comment in Python?
questions.explanation: Everything after # on a line is ignored by the interpreter.

questions.question: What does "Hello"[0] return?
questions.explanation: Strings are indexed from 0, so index 0 is the first character.

questions.question: Which built-in function reads a line of text typed by the user?
questions.explanation: input() waits for the user and returns what they typed as a string.

questions.question: What is the value of 2 ** 3?
questions.explanation: ** is exponentiation: 2 to the power of 3 is 8.

questions.question: Which of these values is falsy in Python?
questions.explanation: The integer 0 is falsy. Non-empty strings and non-empty lists are truthy, even "0" and [0].

questions.question: Which loop runs with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4?
questions.explanation: range(5) produces 0 up to but not including 5.

questions.question: Which list method adds one item to the end of a list?
questions.explanation: list.append(x) adds x at the end; insert(i, x) adds at a position.

questions.question: What does len("abc") return?
questions.explanation: len counts the characters in the string.

questions.question: Which keyword defines a function?
questions.explanation: Functions are written as def name(parameters):

questions.question: What does "a,b,c".split(",") return?
questions.explanation: split cuts the string at each separator and returns a list of the pieces.

questions.question: What does list(enumerate(['x', 'y'])) produce?
questions.explanation: enumerate pairs each item with its index, starting at 0 by default.

questions.question: In def f(*args):, what is args?
options: A tuple of the extra positional arguments
questions.explanation: *args gathers any additional positional arguments into a tuple.

questions.question: In def f(**kwargs):, what is kwargs?
options: A dictionary of extra keyword arguments
questions.explanation: **kwargs collects keyword arguments that were not matched by name into a dict.

questions.question: nums = [3, 1, 2]; s = sorted(nums, reverse=True). What are s and nums afterwards?
questions.explanation: sorted returns a new list and leaves the original unchanged; list.sort() would sort in place.

questions.question: What is the result of (lambda x: x * 2)(5)?
questions.explanation: The lambda is called immediately with x = 5 and returns 10.

questions.question: What happens when you open an existing file with open(path, "w")?
options: Text is added at the end
The file's old content is erased
questions.explanation: Mode "w" truncates the file. Use "a" to append.

questions.question: When does the finally block of a try statement run?
options: Always, whether or not an exception occurred
questions.explanation: finally always runs, which makes it the place for cleanup code.

questions.question: What does {x: x * x for x in range(3)} create?
questions.explanation: A dict comprehension builds key: value pairs; here each number maps to its square.

questions.question: What is the difference between a is b and a == b?
options: is checks whether both names refer to the same object; == checks whether the values are equal
questions.explanation: Two equal lists are == but not the same object, so a is b is False.

questions.question: Why is sum(x * x for x in data) preferred over sum([x * x for x in data]) for very large data?
options: The generator expression produces values one at a time instead of building a whole list in memory
Generators are always faster to type-check
questions.explanation: Generator expressions are lazy, so memory use stays constant regardless of input size.

questions.question: What does the @property decorator do on a method?
options: Lets it be read like an attribute (obj.area instead of obj.area())
questions.explanation: @property turns a method into a getter, so computed values look like plain attributes.

options: get is a closure that keeps a reference to n from the enclosing scope
Python copies all variables into every function
questions.explanation: Inner functions capture variables of the enclosing function; that captured environment is a closure.

questions.question: What is the nonlocal keyword used for?
options: To assign to a variable of the enclosing function from a nested function
questions.explanation: Without nonlocal, assigning inside the nested function would create a new local variable.

questions.question: a = [[1, 2]]; b = copy.copy(a); b[0].append(3). What is a now?
questions.explanation: copy.copy is shallow: the outer list is new but the inner list is shared. copy.deepcopy would copy it too.

questions.question: Which two methods must an object define to be used in a with statement?
questions.explanation: with calls __enter__ at the start and __exit__ at the end, even if an exception occurs.

questions.question: Inside an async function, what does await do?
options: Blocks the whole program until the operation finishes
Suspends this coroutine until the awaitable completes, letting the event loop run other tasks
Starts a new operating system thread
Converts the function to synchronous code
questions.explanation: await yields control to the event loop, which is how asyncio runs many I/O-bound tasks concurrently.

questions.question: With multiple inheritance, which order does super() follow to find the next method?
options: The method resolution order (MRO), computed by C3 linearisation
Always the first base class only
questions.explanation: Class.__mro__ shows the order; super() moves to the next class in it, which makes cooperative inheritance work.

questions.question: Which C# type is a value type?
questions.explanation: int (System.Int32) is a struct, so it is a value type. string, object and List<T> are reference types.

questions.question: What does the 'var' keyword do in C#?
options: Lets the compiler infer the static type from the initialiser
questions.explanation: var is implicit typing: the type is still fixed at compile time, inferred from the right-hand side.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'const' and 'readonly' fields?
options: const is set at compile time; readonly can be set at runtime in a constructor
readonly is set at compile time; const can be set in a constructor
const can only be used for strings
questions.explanation: const values are compile-time constants; readonly fields are assigned at declaration or in the constructor.

questions.question: What does numbers.Where(n => n > 2).Select(n => n * 10) return for numbers = {1, 2, 3, 4}?
questions.explanation: Where keeps 3 and 4; Select multiplies each by 10.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'using' statement around an IDisposable object?
options: To call Dispose automatically when the block ends
questions.explanation: using (var x = ...) { } guarantees Dispose is called, even if an exception is thrown.

questions.question: Which access modifier makes a member visible only inside its own class?
questions.explanation: private restricts access to the containing type. protected also allows derived classes.

questions.question: What does 'await' do inside an async method?
options: Blocks the thread until the task finishes
Pauses the method without blocking the thread and resumes when the task completes
questions.explanation: await yields control back to the caller; the rest of the method runs as a continuation when the awaited task completes.

questions.question: What does 'int? x = null;' declare?
questions.explanation: T? on a value type is shorthand for Nullable<T>, which can hold null.

questions.question: A method is declared 'virtual' in a base class. What must a derived class use to replace its behaviour polymorphically?
questions.explanation: override replaces a virtual member so calls through a base reference use the derived implementation; new only hides it.

questions.question: Which collection stores key-value pairs with fast lookup by key?
questions.explanation: Dictionary is a hash table; lookups by key are O(1) on average.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a struct and a class in C#?
options: Structs are value types and are copied on assignment; classes are reference types
Structs are always allocated on the heap
questions.explanation: Assigning a struct copies its data; assigning a class instance copies the reference.

questions.question: Why is StringBuilder preferred over string concatenation inside a large loop?
options: string cannot be concatenated in loops
Strings are immutable, so each concatenation allocates a new string
questions.explanation: Each + on strings creates a new object; StringBuilder appends into a growing buffer.

questions.question: What does an interface in C# contain by default?
options: Member signatures that implementing classes must provide
questions.explanation: An interface defines a contract of members; classes that implement it provide the implementation (default interface methods are an optional later feature).

questions.question: Which method is the usual entry point of a C# console program?
questions.explanation: Execution begins in the static Main method (or in top-level statements, which the compiler turns into one).

questions.question: What does Console.WriteLine("Hi") do?
options: Reads a line from the keyboard
Prints Hi followed by a new line
questions.explanation: WriteLine writes the text to standard output and ends the line; Write would not add the new line.

questions.question: var q = list.Where(x => x > 2); list.Add(5); foreach (var x in q) ... Is 5 included in the loop?
options: No, the query was evaluated when it was created
Yes, LINQ queries are evaluated lazily when enumerated
Only if list is an array
questions.explanation: LINQ to Objects uses deferred execution: the filter runs during enumeration, so items added before the loop are seen.

questions.question: What does await task.ConfigureAwait(false) change?
options: The continuation does not need to resume on the captured synchronization context
It cancels the task on failure
It ignores exceptions from the task
questions.explanation: ConfigureAwait(false) lets the rest of the method continue on any thread-pool thread, which avoids deadlocks and overhead in library code.

questions.question: How does Dispose() differ from a finalizer?
options: Dispose releases resources deterministically when called; a finalizer runs at an unpredictable time during garbage collection
A finalizer runs immediately when the variable goes out of scope
Dispose is called automatically by the garbage collector
questions.explanation: Dispose (often via using) gives deterministic cleanup; finalizers are a non-deterministic safety net run by the GC.

questions.question: Two instances of record Point(int X, int Y) are created with the same X and Y. What does a == b return?
options: false, because they are different objects
true, because records use value-based equality
It depends on the hash code
questions.explanation: Records generate equality members that compare property values, unlike ordinary classes which compare references.

questions.question: Which C# type stores true or false?
questions.explanation: bool (System.Boolean) holds true or false.

questions.question: How do you declare an integer variable x with the value 5?
questions.explanation: The type comes first, then the name and the value; statements end with a semicolon.

questions.question: Which character ends most statements in C#?
questions.explanation: C# statements are terminated with a semicolon.

questions.question: Which line builds the text "Hello Ada" when name is "Ada"?
questions.explanation: The $ prefix enables string interpolation, which replaces {name} with the variable's value.

questions.question: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
questions.explanation: do-while checks the condition after the body, so the body runs before the first check.

questions.question: What is the index of the first element of a C# array?
questions.explanation: C# arrays are zero-based.

questions.question: How do you write a single-line comment in C#?
questions.explanation: // starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; /* */ spans several lines.

questions.question: What does x++ do?
questions.explanation: ++ increments a numeric variable by one.

questions.question: Which keyword creates a new object from a class?
questions.explanation: new calls the constructor and returns the new instance, e.g. var car = new Car();

questions.question: What does a type need so that foreach can loop over it?
options: A GetEnumerator method (for example by implementing IEnumerable)
questions.explanation: foreach works with anything that provides GetEnumerator, which collections get from IEnumerable<T>.

questions.question: What is public int Age { get; set; }?
questions.explanation: The compiler creates a hidden backing field and the get/set accessors.

questions.question: Why choose List<T> over a plain array T[]?
options: A List can grow and shrink as items are added or removed
questions.explanation: Arrays have a fixed length; List<T> resizes its internal array automatically.

questions.question: In a try with several catch blocks, in what order should they be written?
questions.explanation: The first matching catch wins, so catch (Exception) placed first would hide the specific handlers.

questions.question: When does string.IsNullOrEmpty(s) return true?
questions.explanation: It checks both cases; string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace also treats whitespace-only strings as empty.

questions.question: What does customer?.Address do when customer is null?
questions.explanation: ?. is the null-conditional operator: member access is skipped and the expression evaluates to null.

questions.question: What is the value of name ?? "guest" when name is null?
questions.explanation: ?? returns the left operand if it is not null, otherwise the right operand.

questions.question: A static field in a class belongs to...
options: The type itself, shared by all instances
questions.explanation: There is one copy of a static field per type, accessed through the class name.

questions.question: What happens when an int is assigned to a variable of type object?
options: Nothing, int is already an object reference
Boxing: the value is copied into a new object on the heap
The value is converted to a string
questions.explanation: Boxing allocates; doing it in hot loops (e.g. non-generic collections) costs memory and GC time.

questions.question: With Entity Framework, why does filtering an IQueryable<T> differ from filtering an IEnumerable<T>?
options: IQueryable filters are translated into SQL and run in the database; IEnumerable filters run in memory after loading the rows
questions.explanation: Calling AsEnumerable() or ToList() too early pulls the whole table into memory before filtering.

questions.question: What is Span<T> mainly used for?
options: Working with a slice of contiguous memory without copying or allocating
questions.explanation: Span<T> is a stack-only view over arrays, strings or native memory, used in high-performance parsing.

questions.question: Why should async void be avoided except for event handlers?
options: Callers cannot await it, and exceptions thrown inside it cannot be caught by the caller
It uses more memory than async Task
questions.explanation: async Task lets callers await completion and observe exceptions; async void escapes both.

questions.question: What does lock (sync) { ... } guarantee?
options: Only one thread at a time executes code locked on the same object
The block runs on the UI thread
questions.explanation: lock provides mutual exclusion to protect shared state from race conditions.

questions.question: Why can an IEnumerable<string> be assigned to a variable of type IEnumerable<object>?
options: Because string is a value type
It cannot; this is a compile error
questions.explanation: The out keyword marks T as output-only, so a sequence of a derived type can be used as a sequence of its base type.

questions.question: What does the sealed keyword on a class do?
options: Prevents other classes from inheriting from it
questions.explanation: sealed stops inheritance, which also lets the runtime optimise some virtual calls.

questions.question: Why does the .NET garbage collector use generations?
options: Most objects die young, so collecting the youngest generation often is cheap and frees most memory
To run collections only once per program
questions.explanation: Gen 0 collections are frequent and fast; long-lived objects are promoted and checked less often.

questions.question: In ASP.NET Core dependency injection, what does a Scoped service lifetime mean?
options: One instance for the whole application
A new instance every time it is requested
questions.explanation: Singleton is one per app, Transient is new each time, Scoped is one per request scope (typical for DbContext).

questions.question: Which clause filters rows before grouping?
questions.explanation: WHERE filters individual rows; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY.

questions.question: Which statement returns the number of rows in the table orders?
questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows.

questions.question: What does a LEFT JOIN return?
options: Only rows that match in both tables
All rows from the left table, with matching right rows or NULLs
All rows from the right table only
questions.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps every left row; columns from the right table are NULL where no match exists.

questions.question: Which query lists each customer_id with its number of orders, only for customers with more than 5 orders?
options: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 GROUP BY customer_id
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
SELECT customer_id FROM orders HAVING customer_id > 5
questions.explanation: Aggregates cannot be used in WHERE; conditions on groups go in HAVING.

questions.question: What does a PRIMARY KEY guarantee?
options: Values are unique and not NULL
The column is indexed as text
The column can reference another table
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.

questions.question: Which condition correctly finds rows where email has no value?
questions.explanation: NULL is not equal to anything, not even NULL, so comparisons must use IS NULL.

questions.question: What is a FOREIGN KEY used for?
options: Linking a column to the primary key of another table to keep references valid
questions.explanation: A foreign key enforces referential integrity between related tables.

questions.question: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a SELECT result?
questions.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns each distinct row once.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of an index on a column?
options: To speed up searches and joins on that column
To hide the column from queries
questions.explanation: Indexes let the database find rows without scanning the whole table, at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.

questions.question: What happens to all changes in a transaction when ROLLBACK is executed?
options: Only the last statement is undone
They are written to a log and kept
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK undoes every change made since the transaction began; COMMIT makes them permanent.

questions.question: What does UNION do, compared with UNION ALL?
options: UNION keeps duplicates, UNION ALL removes them
UNION removes duplicate rows, UNION ALL keeps them
UNION joins columns side by side
questions.explanation: UNION combines result sets and removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps every row and is faster.

questions.question: Why are parameterised queries used instead of building SQL strings from user input?
options: They run faster on every database
They prevent SQL injection by sending data separately from the SQL code
They avoid the need for indexes
questions.explanation: Parameters are never interpreted as SQL, so input such as ' OR 1=1 -- cannot change the query.

questions.question: Which clause sorts the result from highest to lowest salary?
questions.explanation: ORDER BY column DESC sorts in descending order; ASC (the default) sorts ascending.

questions.question: Which statement adds a new row to a table?
questions.explanation: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (...) adds rows; UPDATE changes existing rows.

questions.question: What does ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) produce?
options: The total number of rows in the table
A running number restarting at 1 in each department, ordered by salary
questions.explanation: A window function computes values over a partition without collapsing rows; here it ranks employees within each department.

questions.question: Which is the lowest standard isolation level that prevents dirty reads?
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED only shows committed data. Higher levels also prevent non-repeatable reads and phantoms.

questions.question: What is a covering index for a query?
options: An index on every column of the table
An index that contains all columns the query needs, so the table itself need not be read
An index that is rebuilt automatically
questions.explanation: If every referenced column is in the index, the database can answer from the index alone (an index-only scan).

questions.question: What does EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE) show for a query?
options: The execution plan: scans, joins and estimated or actual costs
questions.explanation: Reading the plan shows whether indexes are used and where time goes, which is the starting point for query tuning.

questions.question: Which statement changes values in existing rows?
questions.explanation: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE ... modifies existing rows; ALTER changes the table structure.

questions.question: Which statement removes rows from a table?
questions.explanation: DELETE FROM table WHERE ... removes rows; DROP TABLE removes the whole table.

questions.question: What does SELECT * FROM users return?
questions.explanation: * means every column; without WHERE every row is returned.

questions.question: Which operator is used to match a text pattern?
questions.explanation: LIKE compares against a pattern such as 'An%'.

questions.question: Which function returns the largest value in a column?
questions.explanation: MAX returns the maximum; MIN the minimum.

questions.question: Which keyword requires two conditions to both be true?
questions.explanation: WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 keeps only rows that satisfy both conditions.

questions.question: Which statement creates a new table?
questions.explanation: CREATE TABLE name (column type, ...) defines a new table.

questions.question: In SELECT first_name AS name FROM users, what does AS do?
options: Gives the column a different name in the result
questions.explanation: AS creates an alias for a column or table.

questions.question: In a LIKE pattern, which wildcard matches any sequence of characters?
questions.explanation: % matches zero or more characters; _ matches exactly one.

questions.question: What does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Only rows that have a match in both tables
All rows from the left table
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN keeps pairs of rows that satisfy the join condition.

questions.question: Does WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20 include rows where price is exactly 10 or 20?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends.

questions.question: What does WHERE city IN ('Ankara', 'Izmir') do?
options: Keeps rows whose city is Ankara or Izmir
Keeps rows whose city contains both words
questions.explanation: IN checks whether a value equals any item in the list.

questions.question: SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE city = 'Ankara') returns...
options: Employees who work in a department located in Ankara
Nothing, subqueries are not allowed in WHERE
questions.explanation: The subquery lists Ankara department ids and the outer query keeps employees in those departments.

questions.question: How does COUNT(email) differ from COUNT(*)?
options: COUNT(email) skips rows where email is NULL
questions.explanation: Aggregates over a column ignore NULLs; COUNT(*) counts rows.

questions.question: SELECT dept, name, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept is rejected by standard SQL. Why?
options: name is neither grouped nor aggregated, so its value per group is undefined
GROUP BY must come before FROM
questions.explanation: Every selected column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function.

questions.question: What does First Normal Form (1NF) require?
options: Every table has a foreign key
Each column holds atomic values, with no lists or repeating groups in one cell
questions.explanation: Storing 'Python, SQL' in one cell breaks 1NF; use a separate row or table per value.

questions.question: What is a CASE expression used for?
options: Returning different values depending on conditions, like if/else inside a query
questions.explanation: Example: CASE WHEN score >= 60 THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END.

questions.question: An employees table has a manager_id column pointing to another employee. How do you list each employee with their manager's name?
options: Join the table to itself (a self join) with two aliases
It is impossible without a second table
questions.explanation: FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id.

questions.question: What does a WITH clause (common table expression) provide?
options: A named temporary result set usable in the following query, optionally recursive
questions.explanation: CTEs make complex queries readable and allow recursion.

questions.question: Which problem is a recursive CTE well suited to?
options: Walking a hierarchy, such as every report under a manager at any depth
questions.explanation: The recursive part joins back to the CTE until no new rows appear.

questions.question: Two transactions each hold a lock the other is waiting for. What usually happens?
options: The database detects the deadlock and aborts one transaction
questions.explanation: The victim is rolled back and should be retried; consistent lock ordering reduces deadlocks.

questions.question: Which isolation level prevents phantom reads in the SQL standard?
questions.explanation: Only SERIALIZABLE guarantees that re-running a range query sees no new rows inserted by others.

questions.question: A composite index on (last_name, first_name) exists. Which query can use it efficiently?
questions.explanation: B-tree indexes are used from the leftmost column; first_name alone cannot seek into this index.

questions.question: What is the trade-off of denormalising a schema?
options: Faster reads with fewer joins, at the cost of duplicated data and harder updates
Less disk space and faster writes
It removes the need for indexes
questions.explanation: Reporting tables are often denormalised; the redundancy must be kept consistent.

questions.question: Why can WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024 be slow even with an index on created_at?
options: YEAR() is not a real function
Wrapping the column in a function stops the index from being used; a range like created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01' can use it
questions.explanation: Conditions that keep the column bare are 'sargable' and allow index seeks.

questions.question: How does optimistic concurrency control usually detect conflicting updates?
options: By locking every row it reads
By checking a version or timestamp column in the UPDATE's WHERE clause and failing if it changed
By running all transactions one at a time
questions.explanation: If zero rows are updated, someone else changed the row first and the client retries or reports a conflict.

questions.question: In ACID, what does Durability guarantee?
options: Once a transaction commits, its changes survive crashes and power loss
questions.explanation: Durability is usually provided by a write-ahead log flushed to disk before the commit is confirmed.

questions.question: What is encapsulation?
options: Creating many objects from one class
Hiding internal state and exposing behaviour through a public interface
questions.explanation: Encapsulation keeps data private and controls access through methods, so invariants can be protected.

questions.question: Which relationship does inheritance usually model?
questions.explanation: A Dog is an Animal: inheritance models is-a. has-a is usually modelled with composition.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: Calling the same method on different types and getting type-specific behaviour
questions.explanation: With polymorphism, code written against a base type works with any subtype, each providing its own implementation.

questions.question: What is an abstract class?
options: A class that cannot have methods
A class that cannot be instantiated directly and may contain abstract members
A class with only static members
questions.explanation: Abstract classes define shared behaviour and leave some members for subclasses to implement.

questions.question: What does 'favour composition over inheritance' recommend?
options: Build behaviour by combining objects instead of deep class hierarchies
Always inherit from at least two classes
questions.explanation: Composition keeps classes loosely coupled and lets behaviour change at runtime.

questions.question: What is a constructor?
options: A method that destroys an object
A special method that initialises a new object
questions.explanation: A constructor runs when an object is created and sets up its initial state.

questions.question: Which SOLID principle says a class should have only one reason to change?
questions.explanation: The Single Responsibility Principle keeps each class focused on one job.

questions.question: The Liskov Substitution Principle states that...
options: Subclasses should be usable anywhere their base class is expected without breaking correctness
Classes should depend on concrete implementations
Classes should be closed for extension
questions.explanation: If code works with a base type, it must also work with any subtype; a Square overriding Rectangle setters is a classic violation.

questions.question: Dependency Inversion suggests that high-level modules should depend on...
questions.explanation: Both high- and low-level code depend on abstractions, which makes it possible to swap implementations and test in isolation.

questions.question: Which design pattern ensures a class has only one instance?
questions.explanation: Singleton restricts instantiation to one object and provides a global access point.

questions.question: Which pattern lets objects subscribe to and be notified of changes in another object?
questions.explanation: In Observer, a subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them when its state changes.

questions.question: Which pattern selects an algorithm at runtime by passing in an object that implements a common interface?
questions.explanation: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface.

questions.question: What is method overloading?
options: Redefining a base-class method in a subclass
Several methods with the same name but different parameter lists
Calling a method too many times
questions.explanation: Overloading is resolved at compile time by parameters; overriding replaces a base method at runtime.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
options: An object is an instance created from a class
A class is created from an object
A class is a type of variable
questions.explanation: A class is the blueprint; each object built from it has its own state.

questions.question: Inside a method, what does this (C#, Java) or self (Python) refer to?
options: The current object the method was called on
questions.explanation: It is a reference to the instance whose method is running, used to reach its fields and other methods.

questions.question: What is a field (attribute) of a class?
options: A method that returns a value
A variable that stores part of an object's state
questions.explanation: Fields hold the data of each object, for example a Car's speed or colour.

questions.question: The Open/Closed Principle says software entities should be...
options: Open for modification, closed for extension
Open for extension, closed for modification
Open source and closed for sale
questions.explanation: New behaviour should be added by extending (new classes, implementations) rather than editing tested code.

questions.question: Which principle advises many small, client-specific interfaces instead of one large interface?
questions.explanation: Interface Segregation keeps classes from depending on methods they do not use.

questions.question: What is a main benefit of dependency injection?
options: Classes receive their dependencies from outside, so implementations can be swapped, for example with fakes in tests
It removes the need for interfaces
questions.explanation: Injecting dependencies decouples classes from concrete implementations and makes unit testing straightforward.

questions.question: Which pattern adds behaviour to an object by wrapping it in another object with the same interface?
questions.explanation: A decorator implements the same interface, holds the original object and adds work before or after delegating to it.

questions.question: What is inheritance?
options: A class receiving the fields and methods of another class
questions.explanation: A subclass inherits members from its parent and can add or change behaviour.

questions.question: What is a method?
options: A function that belongs to a class or object
questions.explanation: Methods define what an object can do, e.g. car.drive().

questions.question: What does marking a member private mean?
options: It can be used from anywhere
It can only be accessed inside its own class
It can only be read, never changed
questions.explanation: private hides implementation details and protects the object's state.

questions.question: Given a class Car, which of these is an object?
options: myCar, a specific red Car created with new Car()
questions.explanation: Objects are concrete instances; the class is only the description.

questions.question: What is a getter?
options: A method that returns the value of a field
A method that deletes an object
questions.explanation: Getters give controlled read access to private data; setters give controlled write access.

questions.question: If class Dog extends Animal, what is Dog?
questions.explanation: Dog is the child (subclass); Animal is the parent (superclass).

questions.question: In Python, how does a subclass call its parent's __init__?
questions.explanation: super() returns a proxy to the parent so its methods can be called.

questions.question: In simple terms, what is an interface?
options: A contract that lists methods a class promises to implement
A finished class with all code
questions.explanation: Code can depend on the interface without knowing which class implements it.

questions.question: What does it mean when a subclass overrides a method?
options: It provides its own version of a method inherited from the parent
questions.explanation: When called on the subclass, its own version runs instead of the parent's.

questions.question: Which combination indicates good class design?
questions.explanation: Classes should depend little on each other (low coupling) and have focused responsibilities (high cohesion).

questions.question: How does composition differ from aggregation?
options: In composition the parts cannot exist without the whole; in aggregation they can
questions.explanation: A House composes its Rooms; a Team aggregates Players who exist on their own.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Factory pattern?
options: To create objects without the caller naming the concrete class
To make a class have one instance
questions.explanation: The factory decides which implementation to build, so callers depend only on an abstraction.

questions.question: Why declare a method parameter as an interface type (e.g. IRepository) instead of a concrete class?
options: Any implementation can be passed, including test doubles
It is required by the compiler
questions.explanation: Programming to interfaces keeps code flexible and testable.

questions.question: What is an immutable object?
options: An object that cannot be created
An object whose state cannot change after it is created
An object stored in a database
questions.explanation: Immutable objects are thread-safe and easy to reason about; changes produce new objects.

questions.question: What does the 'Tell, Don't Ask' guideline suggest?
options: Always ask the user for input
Ask an object to perform work instead of pulling its data out and deciding for it
questions.explanation: account.withdraw(amount) keeps the rule inside the object, instead of checking its balance outside.

questions.question: When is the Builder pattern useful?
options: When an object needs exactly one instance
When constructing an object with many optional parts step by step
When objects must observe each other
questions.explanation: A builder avoids constructors with long parameter lists.

questions.question: What does the Template Method pattern do?
options: A base class defines the steps of an algorithm and subclasses fill in some steps
Creates objects from a template file
questions.explanation: The overall order stays fixed in the base class; only specific steps vary.

questions.question: What is the 'fragile base class' problem?
options: Seemingly safe changes in a base class break subclasses that depend on its internal behaviour
questions.explanation: Deep inheritance couples subclasses to implementation details; composition reduces this risk.

questions.question: Which call chain violates the Law of Demeter?
questions.explanation: Reaching through several objects couples the caller to the whole structure; ask the nearest object instead.

questions.question: Which pattern lets a class with an incompatible interface work where another interface is expected?
questions.explanation: An adapter wraps the existing class and translates calls into the expected interface.

questions.question: What problem does the Visitor pattern solve?
options: Adding new operations over a fixed set of classes without changing those classes
questions.explanation: Each operation becomes a visitor; elements accept visitors via double dispatch.

questions.question: Which pattern represents a request as an object, making undo and queuing possible?
questions.explanation: Command objects can be stored, queued, logged and reversed.

questions.question: What is an 'anemic domain model'?
options: A model with too many methods
Domain classes that only hold data, with all behaviour placed in separate services
questions.explanation: It loses encapsulation: rules about the data live far from the data.

questions.question: In Python, what is a mixin class?
options: A class that must be instantiated alone
A small class that adds a focused set of methods to others through multiple inheritance
An abstract base class with no methods
questions.explanation: For example a JsonMixin providing to_json() can be combined with unrelated classes.

questions.question: What does Command-Query Separation (CQS) state?
options: Commands must run in a separate thread
A method should either change state or return data, but not both
Every class needs a command line
questions.explanation: Separating them makes side effects visible and queries safe to call repeatedly.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
questions.explanation: Each step halves the search range, so about log2(n) steps are needed.

questions.question: Which data structure follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order?
questions.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added element first; a queue is FIFO.

questions.question: What is the average time complexity of looking up a key in a hash table?
questions.explanation: Hashing maps a key directly to a bucket; with few collisions lookups are constant time on average.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of quicksort?
questions.explanation: With consistently bad pivots (for example an already sorted array and first-element pivot), quicksort degrades to O(n^2); its average is O(n log n).

questions.question: Which algorithm finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
questions.explanation: BFS explores nodes level by level, so the first time it reaches a node is via a shortest path in edge count.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of accessing the element at index i of an array?
questions.explanation: Array elements are stored contiguously, so the address of element i is computed directly.

questions.question: In a binary search tree, where are values smaller than a node stored?
questions.explanation: BST property: left subtree < node < right subtree, which makes in-order traversal sorted.

questions.question: Which technique stores results of subproblems to avoid recomputing them?
questions.explanation: Dynamic programming (memoisation or tabulation) reuses overlapping subproblem results, e.g. Fibonacci in O(n).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of merge sort in all cases?
questions.explanation: Merge sort always splits in half (log n levels) and merges in linear time per level.

questions.question: Which structure is best for always retrieving the smallest element quickly?
questions.explanation: A min-heap returns the minimum in O(1) and removes it in O(log n).

questions.question: Two nested loops, each running n times, have what time complexity?
questions.explanation: The inner body runs n * n times.

questions.question: What does a recursive function need to avoid infinite recursion?
options: A base case that stops the recursion
questions.explanation: Each recursive call must move towards a base case that returns without recursing.

questions.question: What is the cost of inserting at the head of a singly linked list?
questions.explanation: Only the new node's next pointer and the head pointer change, regardless of list length.

questions.question: Which data structure works First-In-First-Out (FIFO)?
questions.explanation: A queue removes elements in the order they were added, like a line at a ticket office.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of linear search in an unsorted list of n items?
questions.explanation: In the worst case every element must be checked once.

questions.question: When can Dijkstra's algorithm give wrong shortest paths?
options: When some edge weights are negative
When the graph is very large
questions.explanation: Dijkstra assumes a settled node's distance never improves, which negative edges break; use Bellman-Ford instead.

questions.question: Appending to a dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full costs, amortised over many appends...
questions.explanation: Resizing copies n items only after n cheap appends, so the average cost per append stays constant.

questions.question: A topological sort of a graph exists only if the graph...
questions.explanation: A cycle makes it impossible to put every node after all its prerequisites; this is how build tools detect circular dependencies.

questions.question: What is the worst-case lookup time in a hash table, and when does it happen?
options: O(n), when many keys collide into the same bucket
O(log n), when the table is full
questions.explanation: With heavy collisions a bucket degrades to a list scan; good hash functions and resizing keep the average at O(1).

questions.question: What does Big-O notation describe?
options: The exact running time in seconds
How running time or memory grows as the input size grows
The number of lines of code
questions.explanation: Big-O ignores constants and focuses on the growth rate, e.g. O(n) vs O(n^2).

questions.question: What is [3, 1, 2] after sorting in ascending order?
questions.explanation: Ascending means from smallest to largest.

questions.question: push and pop are the main operations of which structure?
questions.explanation: push adds to the top of a stack and pop removes from the top.

questions.question: What does binary search require of the data?
options: It must fit in one line
questions.explanation: Binary search halves the range by comparing with the middle element, which only works on sorted data.

questions.question: What does a node in a singly linked list contain?
options: A value and a reference to the next node
questions.explanation: Nodes are connected through next references; the last node points to null.

questions.question: For large inputs, which is usually faster?
questions.explanation: n grows much more slowly than n squared as n increases.

questions.question: What is a recursive function?
options: A function defined inside a loop
questions.explanation: Recursion solves a problem by solving smaller instances of the same problem.

questions.question: In a tree, what is the root?
options: The top node, which has no parent
questions.explanation: Nodes without children are leaves; the single node without a parent is the root.

questions.question: What is a graph made of?
questions.explanation: Graphs model networks such as roads, friendships or dependencies.

questions.question: Which structure does depth-first search (DFS) use, explicitly or through recursion?
questions.explanation: DFS goes deep along one path before backtracking, which is stack behaviour; BFS uses a queue.

questions.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort?
questions.explanation: It compares neighbouring pairs in up to n passes over the array.

questions.question: In a sorted array, the two-pointer technique finds a pair with a given sum in...
questions.explanation: Move the left pointer right if the sum is too small and the right pointer left if too large; each element is visited once.

questions.question: Using a hash set, detecting whether a list of n items has duplicates takes on average...
questions.explanation: Each item is checked and inserted in O(1) average time.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting into a binary heap of n elements?
questions.explanation: The new element bubbles up at most the height of the tree, which is log n.

questions.question: Searching a binary search tree is O(log n) when it is balanced. What is the worst case if it is not balanced?
questions.explanation: Inserting sorted values creates a chain like a linked list; balanced trees (AVL, red-black) avoid this.

questions.question: How much extra memory does a standard merge sort on an array use?
questions.explanation: Merging needs a temporary array proportional to the input.

questions.question: Computing the n-th Fibonacci number recursively with memoisation takes...
questions.explanation: Each value from 0 to n is computed once and then reused.

questions.question: Why do many quicksort implementations choose the pivot randomly?
options: To make the O(n^2) worst case on already sorted input very unlikely
To use less memory than merge sort in every case
questions.explanation: A random pivot gives O(n log n) expected time regardless of input order.

questions.question: What is the lower bound for any comparison-based sorting algorithm in the worst case?
questions.explanation: There are n! possible orders and each comparison gives one bit, so about log2(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons are needed.

questions.question: With union by rank and path compression, the amortised cost of a Union-Find operation is...
questions.explanation: The inverse Ackermann function grows so slowly that it is below 5 for any practical input.

questions.question: What does Kruskal's algorithm find?
options: The shortest path between two nodes
A minimum spanning tree of a weighted graph
questions.explanation: It adds the cheapest edges that do not create a cycle, often using Union-Find.

questions.question: Which two properties make a problem suitable for dynamic programming?
questions.explanation: Optimal answers are built from optimal sub-answers, and the same subproblems repeat so caching pays off.

questions.question: Coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6: the greedy choice (always take the largest coin) uses 4+1+1. Why does this show greedy is not always optimal?
options: Greedy is always optimal for coins
3+3 uses only two coins, so the greedy answer of three coins is not minimal
6 cannot be made from these coins
questions.explanation: Greedy only works when the problem has the greedy-choice property; otherwise use dynamic programming.

questions.question: Which data structure is best for autocomplete (finding all words with a given prefix)?
questions.explanation: A trie walks down one character per level, so a prefix lookup costs time proportional to the prefix length.

questions.question: What can a Bloom filter answer incorrectly?
options: It can say an item is absent when it was added
It can say an item might be present when it was never added (false positive)
It always needs O(n) memory per item
questions.explanation: Bloom filters have no false negatives but some false positives, in exchange for very small memory use.

questions.question: When does A* search guarantee finding a shortest path?
options: When the graph has no cycles
When its heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost (admissible)
Never; it only finds some path
questions.explanation: An admissible heuristic keeps A* optimal while exploring far fewer nodes than Dijkstra.
